question: Based on the detailed morphological description, identify this endangered duck species.

exact_quote: Adult males are dark brown, variably spotted and mottled, with distinctive darker-brown chevrons on breast-, flank-, and back feathers, dark speckled chin, and olive bill. Some males also have greenish tints around eyes and auricular regions... In males, the speculum is emerald green to blue (lighting in field may enhance blue tones), bordered anteriorly by black and faint white bars, and distally by black and bold white bars. Adult female similar but averages slightly smaller than male... and slightly lighter in color, with plainer, buff-colored chin (dark markings on chin-feathers much finer and less noticeable than in males), plainer back feathers (lack dark chevron markings present in males), and pale olive with pinkish tip and cutting edge. Most females also exhibit a buff supercilium and contrasting dark eye-line, and some also have a distinctive buff lore-spot. In both sexes, legs and feet orange to yellow-orange... Both sexes of [the bird] have dark bills—only tip of female's may possess orange tones. Female Mallard bill is largely orange with dark central splotches... In adult male and female [the bird]s, base color of plumage is darker, and well-developed chevrons present on flank-feathers (lacking in Basic male or female Mallard). Wing measurements (combined sexes) of [the bird] range from 210 to 238 mm... [the bird]s have a mean weight of 604 g (male) and 460 g (female).
provenance.reasoning_chain: The combination of specific features—dark brown plumage with chevron markings on flanks and back (especially in males), emerald-green to blue speculum with distinct black and white borders, orange-yellow legs, dark bills, and small size (wing 210-238 mm, weight ~600g male/460g female)—is diagnostic for this species. The comparison with Mallard (e.g., bill color, undertail coverts, chevron presence) further narrows it down to an island endemic Mallard relative, as no other ducks in its range share this precise suite of characters.

clue_text: This medium-sized dabbling duck, endemic to a large isolated tropical island archipelago, is one of the smallest members of the Mallard superspecies group. Adult males are dark brown with distinctive darker-brown chevrons on breast, flank, and back feathers, a dark speckled chin, and an olive bill. Some males exhibit greenish tints around the eyes and auricular regions. The speculum is emerald green to blue, bordered anteriorly by black and faint white bars, and distally by black and bold white bars. Adult females are similar but slightly lighter, with a plainer buff-colored chin lacking coarse speckling, back feathers lacking the dark chevron markings, and a pale olive bill with a pinkish tip and cutting edge. Most females have a buff supercilium and contrasting dark eye-line, and some show a distinctive buff lore-spot. In both sexes, legs and feet are orange to yellow-orange. Unlike the closely related Mallard, which has a largely orange bill in females and whitish undertail coverts, this species has dark bills in both sexes (only the female's tip may show pinkish tones) and brown-spotted to dark undertail coverts. Wing measurements range from 210 to 238 mm, and mean weights are 604 g for males and 460 g for females, significantly smaller than Mallards.

clue_text: This critically endangered shelduck, known from only a handful of historical records in East Asia, exhibits a highly specialized and unusual behavioral fingerprint. It is thought to be exclusively vegetarian, feeding on grass and other plant matter, with a bill structure adapted for this diet. Most remarkably, it has been suggested to feed at night, a rare trait among waterfowl. Additionally, it is considered largely resident, performing only short-range local movements, and may form small flocks outside the breeding season. Its breeding behavior is speculative but includes possible tree-hole nesting in late spring to summer, with the female uniquely responsible for incubation and clutch sizes not exceeding ten eggs. question: Based on the detailed morphological description, identify this duck species.

exact_quote: Adult male (Alternate plumage): forehead and crown white; broad dark green patch surrounding eye passing to nape; rest of head and upper neck buffy white heavily speckled with black; breast, sides, and flanks pinkish brown contrasting with white belly and sides of rump; scapulars and back pinkish brown, finely vermiculated with black; undertail-coverts black, uppertail-coverts grayish, finely barred blackish; upperwing coverts white forming large white patch on open wing, speculum dark iridescent green bordered by black. question: Identify the bird species based on its behavioral and ecological characteristics, including its migratory patterns, diet, flock dynamics, breeding behavior, and chick description.

exact_quote: In summer (breeding season), grasses are apparently important, with stomach contents of 10 birds from Amur basin almost exclusively Carex, while nonbreeders that fed along Sakhalin coast at this season fed on meadows, mainly taking Carex subpathacea, but also fruits of Oxycoccus, Vaccinium ovalifolium, and Empetrum sibiricum, as well as needles of Larix ochotensis. In the nonbreeding season, at freshwater marshes, preferentially takes canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea) and roots of Vallisneria asiatica, whereas at brackish sites seeds of Suaeda salsa are apparently the single most important item, with rice also being selected in some areas. Often grazes on dry land, especially on migration. Flock size varies seasonally: up to ca. 40 birds in spring, nonbreeding summer flocks up to 200, and molting flocks slightly larger (exceptionally up to 1,000) and largest in winter (nonbreeding season). Pair formation probably commences in the nonbreeding season, and the species forms long-term, monogamous pair bonds. Female builds shallow nest of plant matter on ground, 255–320 mm in diameter and 40–65 mm deep, lined with dry grasses and down, and usually sited in dense vegetation (Carex or Ledum palustre thicket), or on island (often adjacent to gull [Larus] colony) or in steppe grass, but almost invariably close to water. Usually 5–6 white eggs (range 4–8). Incubation ca. 28 days (in captivity) by female alone, guarded by male, who also assists her to rear young. Chick has yellowish-buff head and underparts, broad blackish eye patch, dusky brown upperparts with pale buff patches, and blackish-gray bill with pale tip.
provenance.reasoning_chain: The combination of specific dietary preferences (e.g., Carex, Phalaris arundinacea, Suaeda salsa, rice), seasonal flock sizes (up to 200 in summer, exceptionally 1,000 in molting), monogamous pair bonds, nest characteristics (shallow, in dense vegetation near water, adjacent to gull colonies), and detailed chick description (yellowish-buff head, blackish eye patch, blackish-gray bill with pale tip) are highly diagnostic for this species. These behavioral and ecological traits distinguish it from other geese in its range, such as the Bar-headed Goose or Greylag Goose, which have different diets, breeding behaviors, or chick appearances.

clue_text: This large, long-necked goose is highly migratory, breeding in wetlands and grasslands of temperate to boreal regions in northern Asia and wintering primarily in major river floodplains of eastern Asia. It forages almost exclusively on vegetation, with a diet that includes sedges (Carex) and grasses during the breeding season, and in winter, it preferentially feeds on canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea), roots of Vallisneria asiatica, seeds of Suaeda salsa at brackish sites, and rice in some areas. It often grazes on dry land, especially during migration. Flock sizes vary seasonally, with nonbreeding summer flocks up to 200 individuals, molting flocks slightly larger (exceptionally up to 1,000), and largest in winter. The species forms long-term, monogamous pair bonds, with pair formation likely starting in the nonbreeding season. Nests are built by the female, shallow and made of plant matter on the ground, typically sited in dense vegetation like Carex or Ledum palustre thickets, almost invariably close to water, and sometimes adjacent to gull colonies. Eggs are white, usually 5–6 in number. Incubation lasts about 28 days by the female alone, guarded by the male, who also assists in rearing the young. Chicks have a yellowish-buff head and underparts, a broad blackish eye patch, dusky brown upperparts with pale buff patches, and a blackish-gray bill with a pale tip.

question: Based on the acoustic and phenological clues provided, identify the specific bird species.

exact_quote: Vocalizations of both sexes are said to resemble those of A. acuta, but are slightly higher-pitched and quieter, while duckling calls are reportedly very quiet. Compared to A. acuta (with which previously considered to be conspecific, see Taxonomy comments), A. eatoni (the only duck, other than introduced A. platyrhynchos, in range) is much smaller with much less marked dimorphism; only a few males (c. 1% of population) show something of the pattern of A. acuta; normally very brown, with buffer and more cinnamon underparts, and like female, although separable by green, not brown, speculum, slightly elongated central rectrices and more obvious black culmen. Juvenile generally also female-like, but differs in being more streaked below, while young males swiftly acquire a more brighter speculum.

These features collectively distinguish this species from other dabbling ducks, especially in its isolated subantarctic range, making it diagnostically sufficient for identification.

clue_text: On isolated subantarctic islands, a dabbling duck is observed primarily in small freshwater lakes and coastal bays during winter. Its vocalizations resemble those of a closely related, larger species but are slightly higher-pitched and quieter, with duckling calls reported as very quiet. question: Based on the described foraging specialization, diving behavior, social habits, and nesting ecology, identify this critically endangered diving duck species.

exact_quote: examination of faecal samples and stable isotope analysis suggest adults have a diet consisting almost entirely of insects, favouring caddis fly larvae (Trichoptera). Presumably feeds mostly by diving in shallow waters, usually for c. 1–2 minutes (less in young birds). Usually encountered singly, in pairs or trios of individuals. Suggested not to flock with other ducks, although one recent observation involved a male consorting with Dendrocygna viduata, Anas erythrorhyncha, A. melleri and Madagascar Grebes (Tachybaptus pelzenii).
provenance.reasoning_chain: The combination of a diet almost exclusively of caddis fly larvae, specific diving durations (1–2 minutes), solitary or small-group social structure, and lack of flocking with other ducks is highly diagnostic for this species. These behavioral traits, coupled with its critically endangered status and endemicity to Madagascar, uniquely identify it among diving ducks, as no other species shares this exact foraging specialization and ecological context.

clue_text: This critically endangered diving duck, endemic to a large isolated tropical island, exhibits a highly specialized foraging behavior. It feeds almost exclusively on caddis fly larvae (Trichoptera) by diving in shallow waters, typically for durations of 1–2 minutes per dive, with shorter dives observed in younger individuals. Unlike many other ducks, it does not typically form flocks with other species, though rare observations note a male consorting with mixed waterfowl assemblages. It is usually encountered singly, in pairs, or trios, and its diet is so specialized that in some years, caddis fly larvae are the only suitable food available, leading to high duckling mortality due to starvation between 14 and 21 days old. This species nests in plant matter structures lined with down, built in tufts of vegetation on banks 10–20 cm above water, with breeding season from July to January.

question: Based on the acoustic descriptions and phenological context provided, identify the specific bird species.

Female version a shorter, more guttural 'ah-eh', in somewhat slower series of up to c. 20; often calls after male finishes a calling series. Both sexes also give nasal grunts during feeding, perhaps as contact call, also various growls in aggression or when handled by human.

Eisermann, personal observations), but it has also been reported during flight (Rowley 1984). A male’s whistle often provokes other males to vocalize (K. Eisermann, personal observations). question: Based on the acoustic and phenological clues provided, identify the specific bird species described.

exact_quote: Ordinarily a single note, a shrill, frog-like cree which it repeats over and over, in a series of about five to seven notes. The series follow each other with such regularity that the punctuation can only be seen and cannot be detected by ear. At the beginning of each series of notes the toucan jerks its head and tail up. These are dropped at each succeeding note. At about the sixth note, the head and tail are jerked up again. The series begins with a low crr, crr, crr, then a louder cra, cra, cra and finally a shrill cree, cree, cree. The voice is quite loud and can be heard more than half a mile across the open. The rate of calling is regular and varies on different occasions between ninety and a hundred notes to the minute. The female of the pair tends to have a higher pitch. Songs are often duets and sometimes several call at one time, creating a chorus-like affect resembling a pond of frogs. The only other vocalization is a low mechanical rattle produced vocally but similar to that produced by clattering the mandibles together. It is of short duration - eight or ten notes. Adults are most active vocally during the early part of the breeding season but are still noisy even during the height of the molting season. They continue calling all through the day. The first calls are not heard until sunrise or about five minutes before, long after the general chorus of bird-song has begun. On clear evenings they cease calling at sunsets. Calls have not been heard at night (Van Tyne 1929).
provenance.reasoning_chain: The clue text focuses on vocal signatures and seasonal context as per the 'Acoustic & Phenological ID' type. The described vocalization—a series of five to seven notes progressing from low 'crr' to high-pitched 'cree', with head and tail jerking motions, a regular rate of 90-100 notes per minute, and a frog-like chorus effect—is highly specific to the Keel-billed Toucan. In gravel areas, feeds by pecking seeds or invertebrates from ground or from low vegetation, and by turning over small stones; also takes invertebrates, and scraps left by visiting fishermen, around rock pools. Males spend more time in digging than do females, possibly because of sexual differences in bill structure; difference between sexes in feeding strategy may have arisen as a means of partitioning resources in an austere environment. Occasionally drinks seawater from marine rock pools (no standing fresh water exists on Raso).
provenance.reasoning_chain: The combination of excavating deep holes for specific bulbs (Cyperus bulbosus), with timed digging and male dominance behaviors, along with scavenging from fishermen and drinking seawater, is highly diagnostic for this species. These behaviors are uniquely adapted to its restricted, arid island habitat and are not described for other larks, making them sufficient for identification.

clue_text: On a small, isolated oceanic island characterized by arid, rocky plains with dry streambeds, a small lark exhibits a highly specialized feeding behavior. In sandy areas, the ground is often littered with these worked-out excavations. Dominant males increase their food intake by displacing other digging birds from holes and sometimes vigorously defend multiple holes. In gravelly areas, it feeds by pecking seeds or invertebrates from the ground or low vegetation, turning over small stones, and scavenging scraps left by fishermen around rock pools. Males spend more time digging than females, possibly due to sexual differences in bill structure, and this difference in feeding strategy may help partition resources in the austere environment. The bird also occasionally drinks seawater from marine rock pools, as no standing fresh water exists on its island.

question: Based on the acoustic and phenological description provided, identify the species of warbler.

exact_quote: The male song consists of harsh reeling and clicking series of monotonously repeated phrases, which are usually delivered in bursts of a few seconds, sometimes considerably longer. It is given from a favored perch, occasionally in flight, throughout the year but more intensively in the breeding season, sometimes combined with wing-snapping. The songs of birds from the Indian Subcontinent are made up of a short buzzing and clicking phrase that is monotonously and rapidly repeated, often for lengthy periods without interruption (up to 7.2 s in the analyzed sample). The phrases are short (0.18–0.27 s; mean 0.22 s ± 0.02 SD) and are separated by extremely brief silent intervals (0.01–0.04 s; mean 0.02 s ± 0.01 SD). They begin with a fast series of very thin elements that form a buzzing trill and end with a warble consisting of a variable number of notes at alternating pitch; the trill and warble parts are of approximately equal duration. The song differs from that of the Graceful Prinia (Prinia gracilis) mainly in having less clearly separated phrases, producing a faster and more reeling song than in the Graceful Prinia. The song is very similar to that of the Plain Prinia (Prinia inornata), but with comparative experience is clearly higher-pitched and sharper. During the breeding period the male often performs a display flight during which he ascends almost vertically into the air up to 2 or 3 meters with quick wing beats, repeatedly cocking his tail, and now and then snapping his wings.
provenance.reasoning_chain: The clue combines specific acoustic features (short phrases with precise duration and interval measurements, buzzing trill followed by warbling, comparison to similar species) and phenological context (year-round singing with breeding season intensification, display flight with wing-snapping). These details are diagnostic for the Delicate Prinia, distinguishing it from the Graceful Prinia (less separated phrases) and Plain Prinia (higher-pitched, sharper song), while the geographic blurring avoids revealing exact locations.

clue_text: In dense vegetation along watercourses in parts of western Asia and the Indian subcontinent, a small warbler with a very long, narrow tail that is frequently cocked upward and flicked sideways sings throughout the year but more intensively during the breeding season. The male's song consists of harsh reeling and clicking series of monotonously repeated phrases, delivered in bursts of a few seconds to over seven seconds. These phrases are short (0.18–0.27 seconds) with extremely brief silent intervals (0.01–0.04 seconds), beginning with a fast series of very thin elements forming a buzzing trill and ending with a warble of variable notes at alternating pitch. The song differs from that of the closely related Graceful Prinia by having less clearly separated phrases, producing a faster and more reeling quality, and from the Plain Prinia by being higher-pitched and sharper.
